source.title: Data Heterogeneity Limits the Scaling Effect of Pretraining in Neural Data Transformers
source.authors: Linxing Jiang; Shirui Chen; Emmanuel Tanumihardja; Xiaochuang Han; Wei-Jia Shi; Eric Shea-Brown; Rajesh P. N. Rao

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, appendices, and references are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how downstream neural-activity prediction changes with pretraining data and reports that heterogeneity weakens scaling and that full-data outcomes fall below extrapolations from smaller runs.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter-count or training-compute scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its own scaling experiments concern neural-data-transformer downstream performance as the number or selection of pretraining sessions changes. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps pretraining data for neural data transformers on mouse spiking data, a non-text modality, and measures held-out-session log-likelihood (bits-per-spike) after finetuning. It argues explicitly that traditional scaling laws do not transfer directly: gains are modest, they plateau, they shrink under heterogeneity, and the full-data model falls below the log-linear extrapolation. This bears on V5. It does not study language models, so the LM-specific versions are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: more pretraining sessions do not by themselves improve downstream neural-model performance. Explicit heterogeneity (brain-region mismatch) and implicit session-to-session heterogeneity limit scaling, so the authors call prior scaling claims premature and urge fine-grained incremental scaling analyses.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps pretraining session counts and session subsets for a neural-data transformer, measuring downstream neural-activity prediction in BPS and choice accuracy. It does not fit language-model held-out cross-entropy power laws over parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by dataset (RS versus BWM), task, heldout session, and pretraining-session selection order. Forward-prediction scaling also plateaus around 80 sessions; the RS session rankings differ substantially across heldout sessions.

fits_no_version.finding: Which pretraining sessions are used (ranked, random, or reverse-ranked) changes both absolute transfer performance and the strength of scaling. Five top-ranked sessions beat the best random-session models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In heterogeneous non-text data, data-scaling curves depend strongly on which data subsets are added, not only on how much.

record.problems: The scaling experiments use one architecture and neural datasets, not language models. Section 3 uses one seed; the paper notes that conclusions may not generalize to other architectures, objectives, modalities, tasks, or species. Several trends and the extrapolation comparisons are presented only in figures without exact values in the text.

untested.parts: All for language models; the extrapolation test is in a neural modality and is recorded under V5.
All; no depth/width sweep at fixed parameters.
All for published LM laws; data-selection dependence is noted only in a neural setting.
Image/video, repeated data, and an explicit power-law fit; compute scaling.

missing.what: Parameter scaling: the 12M NDT outperformed both 8M and larger 24M/38M models on RS; larger models did not improve.
Percentage gain over the 1-session model by session order: ranked-order scaling is clearly weaker, and 5 ranked sessions reach 86% of the 40-ranked-session best.
Per-session scaling curves deviate from session averages, with large cross-session variability.

record.verdict_notes: Only V5 is treated as tested, because the other versions are framed around language models. The extrapolation is a linear regression of BPS on log(trials), not a power-law fit to loss. BPS is a normalized held-out log-likelihood after finetuning, so it counts as a transfer loss. Scale is small: 12M parameters and at most about 33k trials. Section 3 used a single seed.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
Language-model loss extrapolation and power-law fits specifically; the study instead extrapolates neural downstream performance from data-size fits.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Image/video modalities, repeated-data language-model training, fine-tuning and transfer in language models, and power-law fits to neural-model loss.
Language-model downstream tasks and the relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
Parameter-counting choices, compute-optimal allocation, and fitted exponents; the study tests data-set and session-selection dependence, not these other setup choices.
